title: Three proofs of the Leibniz formula
edgeSemantics: Curated mathematical dependencies; a bundle may combine several intermediate lemmas. This is not a complete declaration graph.

routes.name: Mathlib
routes.description: Power series and Abel’s endpoint theorem

nodes.title: Rational interval foundation
nodes.subtitle: Explicit enclosures and shrinking widths
nodes.body: Rational arithmetic, finite sums and explicit error bounds suffice to describe a real value by increasingly precise intervals. Agreement is proved by comparing valid enclosures. Both native routes stay inside this foundation.

nodes.title: Completed real & complex numbers
nodes.subtitle: Completeness, limits and infinite sums
nodes.body: Mathlib works with its completed real numbers and the complex numbers built from them. Its proof uses topological limits and infinite sums, including an existence theorem for the limit of an alternating series.

nodes.title: Geometric arctangent & π
nodes.subtitle: Rational rectangle bounds and exhaustion
nodes.body: The geometric construction encloses the arctangent area A(1) by rational lower and upper bounds. Refinement makes their gap vanish. The existing canonical π is exactly four times this geometric value; neither route defines π by its series.

nodes.title: Finite geometric algebra
nodes.subtitle: Even and odd polynomials bracket the kernel
nodes.body: Finite geometric division gives the polynomial plus an exact signed remainder. On 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 the denominator is positive, so consecutive even and odd partial polynomials bracket 1/(1+x²). This is finite algebra and does not assume convergence of the kernel series at x = 1.

nodes.title: Complex logarithm & trigonometry
nodes.subtitle: Series for log; arctan as an inverse of tan
nodes.body: The complex arctangent is expressed using complex logarithms. Logarithmic Taylor series produce its power series; restriction to the real axis gives the real expansion. Real trigonometry also supplies continuity of arctan and the endpoint identity arctan(1) = π/4.

nodes.title: Alternating enclosures
nodes.subtitle: Adjacent sums differ by the next term
nodes.body: The magnitudes 1/(2k+1) decrease to zero with an explicit rate. Adjacent alternating sums bound all later sums, giving valid rational intervals. The first omitted term also supplies the classical remainder bound for every inclusive partial sum.

nodes.title: Polynomial primitives
nodes.subtitle: Finite differences certify the power rule
nodes.body: Each monomial has the primitive x^(m+1)/(m+1), with a quantitative finite-difference error bound. Addition and rational scaling assemble these primitive certificates for every finite arctangent polynomial.

nodes.title: Arctangent power series
nodes.subtitle: An identity strictly inside the unit interval
nodes.body: For |x| < 1, the infinite series of odd powers sums to arctan(x). This alone does not permit substituting x = 1: the endpoint is outside this theorem’s hypotheses. Abel’s theorem supplies that missing step.

nodes.title: Finite rectangle estimates
nodes.subtitle: Compare polynomial sums with exact primitives
nodes.body: On each rational cell, finite algebra bounds the difference between a polynomial rectangle sum and the corresponding primitive difference. Summing over a finite partition gives an explicit error controlled by its mesh. No derivative or FTC certificate enters this route.
nodes.formula: rectangle sum = finite primitive sum + bounded error

nodes.title: FTC and integral order
nodes.subtitle: Subdivision removes the finite-difference error
nodes.body: If a polynomial derivative is bounded above or below on a rational cell, its primitive increment obeys the corresponding integral inequality. Repeated subdivision halves the error; an explicit decay bound removes it. This holds for every polynomial degree.

nodes.title: The alternating series converges
nodes.subtitle: Existence of a real limit L
nodes.body: Monotonicity of 1/(2k+1) and convergence to zero give a real limit L for the alternating partial sums. This identifies an existing limit but does not yet identify its value as π/4.

nodes.title: Vanishing error & exhaustion
nodes.subtitle: Finite estimates identify the geometric value
nodes.body: Choose a sufficiently fine rational mesh for each polynomial degree. Its explicit error tends to zero. The polynomial brackets then compare the alternating intervals with the geometric rectangle intervals, proving that both enclose the same value.

nodes.title: Integrate the polynomial brackets
nodes.subtitle: Squeeze the arctangent area between sums
nodes.body: Apply integral order to the finite geometric bounds on each rational cell. The polynomial integrals are the alternating sums of odd reciprocals. Summing the cells brackets the geometric arctangent area between consecutive sums, whose separation tends to zero.

nodes.title: Abel’s endpoint theorem
nodes.subtitle: Pass from the interior power series to x = 1
nodes.body: Abel’s theorem transfers the sum L of the alternating coefficient series to the limit of its power series as the real argument tends to 1 from below. Substituting x² and multiplying by x produces the odd-power arctangent series.

nodes.title: Leibniz: computational proof
nodes.subtitle: Multiply the common geometric value by four
nodes.body: The alternating computation and the canonical geometric π are equivalent. Together with alternating-prefix bounds this also gives |Sₙ − π| ≤ 4/(2n+3), for every inclusive partial sum Sₙ. The proof does not use the FTC comparison.

nodes.title: Leibniz: Taylor / FTC proof
nodes.subtitle: The same canonical π, a separate comparison
nodes.body: The integrated brackets prove agreement with geometric π. The explanatory corollaries express A(1) as its finite Taylor sum plus Rₙ, with |Rₙ| ≤ 1/(2n+3). These remainder statements follow from this route’s equality; they are not prerequisites of that equality.

nodes.title: Leibniz: Mathlib proof
nodes.subtitle: Continuity identifies the endpoint limit
nodes.body: Inside the interval the power series equals arctan. Continuity and uniqueness of limits identify L = arctan(1) = π/4. Mathlib’s theorem states convergence of finite partial sums to π/4 in its real numbers. It is an analogous theorem in a different foundation; this comparison does not add a formal translation between the two π objects.
